entries.c0be00cbdb2fcb06bca992df14b21bd09881e9ae: <div sID="gen20320" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Jonah.2" sID="Jonah.2"/> <div eID="gen20320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20321" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> We left Jonah in the belly of the fish, and had reason to think we should hear no more of him, that if he were not destroyed by the waters of the sea he would be consumed in the bowels of that leviathan, "out of whose mouth go burning lamps, and sparks of fire, and whose breath kindles coals," <reference osisRef="Job.41.19">Job xli. 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.41.21">21</reference>. But God brings his people through fire, and through water (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>); and by his power, behold, Jonah the prophet is yet alive, and is heard of again. In this chapter God hears from him, for we find him praying; in the next Nineveh hears from him, for we find him preaching. In his prayer we have, I. The great distress and danger he was in, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2-Jonah.2.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.6">6</reference>. II. The despair he was thereby almost reduced to, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">ver. 4</reference>. III. The encouragement he took to himself, in this deplorable condition, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">7</reference>. IV. The assurance he had of God's favour to him, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.6-Jonah.2.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. V. The warning and instruction he gives to others, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">ver. 8</reference>. VI. The praise and glory of all given to God, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">ver. 9</reference>. In the <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.10">last verse</reference> we have Jonah's deliverance out of the belly of the fish, and his coming safe and sound upon dry land again.
entries.5bc4d638b6776f7e37112d7e5ae32d333c277534: <div eID="gen20322" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20321" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonah's Prayer; The Prophet in the Fish's Belly. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 840.)</title> <div sID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Jonah prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God out of the fish's belly, <hi type="super">2</hi> And said, I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he heard me; out of the belly of hell cried I, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou heardest my voice. <hi type="super">3</hi> For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight; yet I will look again toward thy holy temple. <hi type="super">5</hi> The waters compassed me about, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the soul: the depth closed me round about, the weeds were wrapped about my head. <hi type="super">6</hi> I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars <hi type="italic">was</hi> about me for ever: yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God. <hi type="super">7</hi> When my soul fainted within me I remembered the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and my prayer came in unto thee, into thine holy temple. <hi type="super">8</hi> They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy. <hi type="super">9</hi> But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay <hi type="italic">that</hi> that I have vowed. Salvation <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20324" type="x-p"/> God and his servant Jonah had parted in anger, and the quarrel began on Jonah's side; he fled from his country that he might outrun his work; but we hope to see them both together again, and the reconciliation begins on God's side. In the close of the foregoing chapter we found God returning to Jonah in a way of mercy, <hi type="italic">delivering him from going down to the pit,</hi> having <hi type="italic">found a ransom;</hi> in this chapter we find Jonah returning to God in a way of duty; he was called up in the former chapter to pray to his God, but we are not told that he did so; however, now at length he is brought to it. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20325" type="x-p"/> I. When he prayed (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then Jonah prayed;</hi> then when he was in trouble, under the sense of sin and the tokens of God's displeasure against him for sin, then he prayed. Note, When we are in affliction we must pray; then we have occasion to pray, then we have errands at the throne of grace and business there; then, if ever, we shall have a disposition to pray, when the heart is humbled, and softened, and made serious; then God expects it (<hi type="italic">in their affliction they will seek me early,</hi> seek me earnestly); and, though we bring our afflictions upon ourselves by our sins, yet, if we pray in humility and godly sincerity, we shall be welcome to the throne of grace, as Jonah was. Then when he was in a hopeful way of deliverance, being preserved alive by miracle, a plain indication that he was reserved for further mercy, then he prayed. An apprehension of God's good-will to us, notwithstanding our offences, gives us boldness of access to him, and opens the lips in prayer which were closed with the sense of guilt and dread of wrath. <div eID="gen20325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20326" type="x-p"/> II. Where he prayed—in <hi type="italic">the fish's belly.</hi> No place is amiss for prayer. <hi type="italic">I will that men pray every where.</hi> Wherever God casts us we may find a way open to heaven-ward, if it be not our own fault. <hi type="italic">Undique ad cœlos tantundem est viæ—The heavens are equally accessible from every part of the earth.</hi> He that has Christ dwelling in his heart by faith, wherever he goes carries the altar along with him, that <hi type="italic">sanctifies the gift,</hi> and is himself a <hi type="italic">living temple.</hi> Jonah was here in confinement; the belly of the fish was his prison, was a close and dark dungeon to him; yet there he had freedom of access to God, and walked at liberty in communion with him. Men may shut us out from communion with one another, but not from communion with God. Jonah was now in the bottom of the sea, yet <hi type="italic">out of the depths he cries to God;</hi> as Paul and Silas prayed in the prison, in the stocks. <div eID="gen20326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20327" type="x-p"/> III. To whom he prayed—<hi type="italic">to the Lord his God.</hi> He had been fleeing from God, but now he sees the folly of it, and returns to him; by prayer he draws near to that God whom he had gone aside from, and <hi type="italic">engages his heart to approach him.</hi> In prayer he has an eye to him, not only as <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> but as <hi type="italic">his God,</hi> a God in covenant with him; for, thanks be to God, every transgression in the covenant does not throw us out of covenant. This encourages even backsliding children to return. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jer. iii. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold, we come unto thee, for thou art the Lord our God.</hi> <div eID="gen20327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20328" type="x-p"/> IV. What his prayer was. He afterwards recollected the substance of it, and left it upon record. He reflects upon the workings of his heart towards God when he was in his distress and danger, and the conflict that was then in his breast between faith and sense, between hope and fear. <div eID="gen20328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20329" type="x-p"/> 1. He reflects upon the earnestness of his prayer, and God's readiness to hear and answer (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">v. 2</reference>): He said, <hi type="italic">I cried, by reason of my affliction, unto the Lord.</hi> Note, Many that prayed not at all, or did but whisper prayer, when they were in prosperity, are brought to pray, nay, are brought to cry, <hi type="italic">by reason of their affliction;</hi> and it is for this end that afflictions are sent, and they are in vain if this end be not answered. Those <hi type="italic">heap up wrath</hi> who <hi type="italic">cry not when God binds them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">Job xxxvi. 13</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Out of the belly of hell</hi> and the grave <hi type="italic">cried I.</hi>" The fish might well be called a grave, and, as it was a prison to which Jonah was condemned for his disobedience and in which he lay under the wrath of God, it might well be called the belly of hell. Thither this good man was cast, and yet thence he cried to God, and it was not in vain; God <hi type="italic">heard him, heard the voice</hi> of his affliction, the voice of his supplication. There is a hell in the other world, out of which there is no crying to God with any hope of being heard; but, whatever hell we may be <hi type="italic">in the belly of</hi> in this world, we may thence <hi type="italic">cry to God.</hi> When Christ lay, as Jonah, three days and three nights in the grave, though he prayed not, as Jonah did, yet his very lying there cried to God for poor sinners, and the cry was heard. <div eID="gen20329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20330" type="x-p"/> 2. He reflects upon the very deplorable condition that he was in when he was in the belly of hell, which, when he lay there, he was very sensible of and made particular remarks upon. Note, If we would get good by our troubles, we must take notice of our troubles, and of the hand of God in them. Jonah observes here, (1.) How low he was thrown (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hadst cast me into the deep.</hi> The mariners cast him there; but he looked above them, and saw the hand of God casting him there. Whatever deeps we are cast into, it is God that casts us into them, and he it is who, <hi type="italic">after he has killed, has power to cast into hell.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">cast into the midst of the seas—the heart of the seas</hi> (so the word is), and thence Christ borrows that Hebrew phrase, when he applies it to his own lying so long in the <hi type="italic">heart of the earth.</hi> For he that is laid dead in the grave, though it be ever so shallow, is cut off as effectually from the land of the living as if he were laid in the <hi type="italic">heart of the earth.</hi> (2.) How terribly he was beset: <hi type="italic">The floods compassed me about.</hi> The channels and springs of the waters of the sea surrounded him on every side; it was always high-water with him. God's dear saints and servants are sometimes encompassed with the floods of affliction, with troubles that are very forcible and violent, that bear down on all before them, and that run constantly upon them, as the waters of a river in a continual succession, one trouble upon the neck of another, as Job's messengers of evil tidings; they are enclosed by them on all sides, as the church complains, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">Lam. iii. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He has hedged me about, that I cannot get out,</hi> nor see which way I may flee for safety. <hi type="italic">All thy billows and thy waves passed over me.</hi> Observe, He calls them God's billows and his waves, not only because he made them (<hi type="italic">the sea is his, and he made it</hi>), and because he <hi type="italic">rules</hi> them (for <hi type="italic">even the winds and the seas obey him</hi>), but because he had now commissioned them against Jonah, and limited them, and ordered them to afflict and terrify him, but not to destroy him. These words are plainly quoted by Jonah from <reference osisRef="Ps.42.7">Ps. xlii. 7</reference>, where, though the translations differ a little, in the original David's complaint is the same <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi>—<hi type="italic">word for word,</hi> with this of Jonah's: <hi type="italic">All thy billows and thy waves passed over me.</hi> What David spoke figuratively and metaphorically Jonah applied to himself as literally fulfilled. For the reconciling of ourselves to our afflictions, it is good to search precedents, that we may find <hi type="italic">there has no temptation taken us but such as is common to men.</hi> If ever any man's case was singular, and not to be paralleled, surely Jonah's was, and yet, to his great satisfaction, he finds even the man after God's own heart making the same complaint of God's <hi type="italic">waves and billows going over him</hi> that he has now occasion to make. When God <hi type="italic">performs the thing that is appointed for us</hi> we shall find that <hi type="italic">many such things are with him,</hi> that even our path of trouble is no untrodden path, and that God deals with us no otherwise than as he <hi type="italic">uses to deal with those that love his name.</hi> And therefore for our assistance in our addresses to God, when we are in trouble, it is good to make use of the complaints and prayers which the saints that have been before us made use of in the like case. See how good it is to be ready in the scriptures; Jonah, when he could make no use of his Bible, by the help of his memory furnished himself from the scripture with a very proper representation of his case: <hi type="italic">All thy billows and thy waves passed over me.</hi> To the same purport, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">v. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">The waters compassed me about even to the soul;</hi> they threatened his life, which was hereby brought into imminent danger; or they made an impression upon his spirit; he saw them to be tokens of God's displeasure, and in them the <hi type="italic">terrors of the Almighty set themselves in array against him;</hi> this reached to his soul, and put that into confusion. And this also is borrowed from David's complaint, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1">Ps. lxix. 1</reference>. The <hi type="italic">waters have come in unto my soul.</hi> When <hi type="italic">without are fightings</hi> it is no marvel that <hi type="italic">within are fears.</hi> Jonah, in the fish's belly, finds the <hi type="italic">depths enclosing him round about,</hi> so that if he would get out of his prison, yet he must unavoidably perish in the waters. He feels the <hi type="italic">sea-weed</hi> (which the fish sucked in with the water) <hi type="italic">wrapped about his head,</hi> so that he has no way left him to help himself, nor hope that any one else can help him. Thus are the people of God sometimes perplexed and entangled, that they may learn not to <hi type="italic">trust in themselves, but in God that raises the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8-2Cor.1.9">2 Cor. i. 8, 9</reference>. (3.) How fast he was held (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.6">v. 6</reference>): He <hi type="italic">went down to the bottom of the mountains,</hi> to the rocks in the sea, upon which the hills and promontories by the seaside seem to be bottomed; he lay among them, nay, he lay under them; the <hi type="italic">earth with her bars was about him,</hi> so close about him that it was likely to be about him for ever. The earth was so shut and locked, so barred and bolted, against him, that he was quite cut off from any hope of ever returning to it. Thus helpless, thus hopeless, did Jonah's case seem to be. Those whom God contends with the whole creation is at war with. <div eID="gen20330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20331" type="x-p"/> 3. He reflects upon the very black and melancholy conclusion he was then ready to make concerning himself, and the relief he obtained against it, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">3v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">7</reference>. (1.) He began to sink into despair, and to give up himself for gone and undone to all intents and purposes. When the <hi type="italic">waters compassed him about even to the soul</hi> no marvel that <hi type="italic">his soul fainted within him,</hi> fainted away, so that he had not any comfortable enjoyments or expectations; his spirits quite failed, and he looked upon himself as a dead man. <hi type="italic">Then I said, I am cast out of thy sight,</hi> and the apprehension of that was the thing that made his spirit faint within him. He thought God had quite forsaken him, would never return in mercy to him, nor show him any token for good again. He had no example before him of any that were brought alive out of a fish's belly; if he thought of Job upon the dunghill, Joseph in the pit, David in the cave, yet these did not come up to his case. Nor was there any visible way of escape open for him but by miracle; and what reason had he to expect that a miracle of mercy should be wrought for him who was now made a monument of justice? His own conscience told him that he had wickedly <hi type="italic">fled from the presence of the Lord,</hi> and therefore he might justly <hi type="italic">cast him away from his presence,</hi> and, in token of that, <hi type="italic">take away his Holy Spirit from him,</hi> never to visit him more. What hopes could he have of deliverance out of a trouble which his <hi type="italic">own ways and doings</hi> had <hi type="italic">procured to himself?</hi> Observe, When Jonah would say the worst he could of his case he says this, <hi type="italic">I am cast out of thy sight;</hi> those, and those only, are miserable, whom God has cast out of his sight, whom he will no longer own and favour. What is the misery of the damned in hell but this, that they are cast out of God's sight? For what is the happiness of heaven but the vision and fruition of God? Sometimes the condition of God's people may be such in this world that they may think themselves quite excluded from God's presence, so as no more to see him, or to be regarded by him. Jacob and Israel said, <hi type="italic">My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa. xl. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Zion said, The Lord has forsaken me, my God has forgotten me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.14">Isa. xlix. 14</reference>. But it is only the surmise of unbelief, for God has not <hi type="italic">cast away his people whom he has chosen.</hi> (2.) Yet he recovered himself from sinking into despair, with some comfortable prospects of deliverance. Faith corrected and controlled the surmises of fear and distrust. Here was a fierce struggle between sense and faith, but faith had the last word and came off a conqueror. In trying times, the issue will be good at last, providing our faith do not fail; it was therefore the continuance of that in its vigour that Christ secured to Peter. <hi type="italic">I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>. David would have fainted if he had not <hi type="italic">believed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Ps. xxvii. 13</reference>. Jonah's faith said, <hi type="italic">Yet I will look again towards thy holy temple.</hi> Thus, though he was <hi type="italic">perplexed,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">not in despair;</hi> in the depth of the sea he had this hope in him, as an <hi type="italic">anchor of the soul, sure and stedfast.</hi> That which he supports himself with the hope of is that he shall yet <hi type="italic">look again towards God's holy temple.</hi> [1.] That he shall live; he shall look again heaven-ward, shall again see the light of the sun, though now he seems to be cast into utter darkness. Thus <hi type="italic">against hope he believed in hope.</hi> [2.] That he shall <hi type="italic">live, and praise God;</hi> and a good man does not desire to live for any other purpose, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.175">Ps. cxix. 175</reference>. That he shall enjoy communion with God again in holy ordinances, shall <hi type="italic">look towards,</hi> and go up to, <hi type="italic">the holy temple,</hi> there <hi type="italic">to enquire,</hi> there to <hi type="italic">behold the beauty of the Lord.</hi> When Hezekiah desired that he might be assured of his recovery, he asked, <hi type="italic">What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the Lord?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.22">Isa. xxxviii. 22</reference>), as if that were the only thing for the sake of which he wished for health; so Jonah here hopes he shall <hi type="italic">look again towards the temple;</hi> that way he had looked many a time with pleasure, rejoicing when he was called <hi type="italic">to go up to the house of the Lord;</hi> and the remembrance of it was his comfort, that, when he had opportunity, he was no stranger to the holy temple. But now he could not so much as look towards it; in the fish's belly he could not tell which way it lay, but he hopes he shall be again able to look towards it, to look on it, to look into it. Observe, How modestly Jonah expresses himself; as one conscious to himself of guilt and unworthiness, he dares not speak of dwelling in God's house, as David, knowing that he is <hi type="italic">no more worthy to be called a son,</hi> but he hopes that he may be admitted to look towards it. He calls it the <hi type="italic">holy temple,</hi> for the holiness of it was, in his eye, the beauty of it, and that for the sake of which he loved and looked towards it. The temple was a type of heaven; and he promises himself that though being now a <hi type="italic">captive exile,</hi> he should never be <hi type="italic">loosed,</hi> but <hi type="italic">die in the pit,</hi> yet he should look towards the heavenly temple, and be brought safely thither. Though he die in the fish's belly, in the bottom of the sea, yet thence he hopes his soul shall be carried by angels into Abraham's bosom. Or these words may be taken as Jonah's vow when he was in distress, and he speaks (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">v. 9</reference>) of paying what he vowed; his vow is that if God deliver him he will praise him <hi type="italic">in the gates of the daughter of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13-Ps.9.14">Ps. ix. 13, 14</reference>. His sin for which God pursued him was <hi type="italic">fleeing from the presence of the Lord,</hi> the folly of which he is now convinced of, and promises not only that he will never again look towards Tarshish, but that he will again look towards the temple, and will go <hi type="italic">from strength to strength</hi> till he appear before God there. And thus we see how faith and hope were his relief in his desponding condition. To these he added prayer to God (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When my soul fainted within me,</hi> then <hi type="italic">I remembered</hi> the Lord, I betook myself to that cordial." He remembered what he is, how nigh to those that seem to be thrown at the greatest distance by trouble, how merciful to those that seem to have thrown themselves at a distance from him by sin. He remembered what he had done for him, what he had done for others, what he could do, what he had promised to do; and this kept him from fainting. Remembering God, he made his addresses to him: "<hi type="italic">My prayer came in unto thee;</hi> I sent it in, and expected to receive an answer to it." Note, Our afflictions should put us in mind of God, and thereby put us upon prayer to him. When our souls faint we must remember God; and, when we remember God, we must send up a prayer to him, a pious ejaculation at least; when we think on his name we should call on his name. <div eID="gen20331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20332" type="x-p"/> 4. He reflects upon the favour of God to him when thus in his distress he sought to God and trusted him. (1.) He graciously accepted his prayer, and gave admission and audience to it (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">My prayer,</hi> being sent to him, <hi type="italic">came in unto him,</hi> even <hi type="italic">into his holy temple;</hi> it was heard in the highest heavens, though it was prayed in the lowest deeps. (2.) He wonderfully wrought deliverance for him, and, when he was in the depth of his misery, gave him the earnest and assurance of it (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption, O Lord my God!</hi> Some think he said this when he was vomited up on dry ground; and then it is the language of thankfulness, and he sets it over-against the great difficulty of his case, that the power of God might be the more magnified in his deliverance: <hi type="italic">The earth with her bars was about me for ever,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">thou hast brought up my life from the pit,</hi> from the <hi type="italic">bars of the pit.</hi> Or, rather, we may suppose it spoken while he was yet in the fish's belly, and then it is the language of his faith: "Thou hast kept me alive here, in the pit, and therefore thou canst, thou wilt, <hi type="italic">bring up my life from the pit;</hi>" and he speaks of it with as much assurance as if it were done already: <hi type="italic">Thou has brought up my life.</hi> Though he has not an express promise of deliverance, he has an earnest of it, and on that he depends: he has life, and therefore believes his life shall be <hi type="italic">brought up from corruption;</hi> and this assurance he addresses to God: <hi type="italic">Thou has done it, O Lord my God!</hi> Thou art the Lord, and therefore <hi type="italic">canst</hi> do it for me, my God, and therefore wilt do it. Note, If the Lord be our God, he will be to us the <hi type="italic">resurrection and the life,</hi> will redeem our lives from destruction, from the power of the grave. <div eID="gen20332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> 5. He gives warning to others, and instructs them to keep close to God (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy,</hi> that is, (1.) Those that worship other gods, as the heathen mariners did, and call upon them, and expect relief and comfort from them, <hi type="italic">forsake their own mercy;</hi> they stand in their own light; they turn their back upon their own happiness, and go quite out of the way of all good. Note, Idols are <hi type="italic">lying vanities,</hi> and those that pay that homage to them which is due to God only act as contrarily to their interests as to their duty. Or, (2.) Those that follow their own inventions, as Jonah himself had done when he <hi type="italic">fled from the presence of the Lord</hi> to go to Tarshish, <hi type="italic">forsake their own mercy,</hi> that mercy which they might find in God, and might have such a covenant-right and title to it as to be able to call it their own, if they would but keep close to God and their duty. Those that think to go any where to be from under the eye of God, as Jonah did—that think to better themselves by deserting his service, as Jonah did—and that grudge his mercy to any poor sinners, and pretend to be wiser than he in judging who are fit to have prophets sent them and who are not, as Jonah did—they <hi type="italic">observe lying vanities,</hi> are led away by foolish groundless fancies, and, like him, they <hi type="italic">forsake their own mercy,</hi> and no good can come of it. Note, Those that forsake their own duty forsake their own mercy; those that run away from the work of their place and day run away from the comfort of it. <div eID="gen20333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20334" type="x-p"/> 6. He solemnly binds his soul with a bond that, if God work deliverance for him, the God of his mercies shall be the God of his praises, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">v. 9</reference>. He covenants with God, (1.) That he will honour him in his devotions with the <hi type="italic">sacrifice of thanksgiving;</hi> and God has said, for the encouragement of those that do so, that those that <hi type="italic">offer praise glorify him.</hi> He will, according to the law of Moses, bring <hi type="italic">a sacrifice of thanksgiving,</hi> and will offer that according to the law of nature, with the <hi type="italic">voice of thanksgiving.</hi> The love and thankfulness of the heart to God are the life and soul of this duty; without these neither the sacrifice of thanksgiving nor the voice of thanksgiving will avail any thing. But gratitude was then, by a divine appointment, to be expressed by a sacrifice, in which the offerer presented the beast slain to God, not in lieu of himself, but in token of himself; and it is now to be expressed by the <hi type="italic">voice of thanksgiving,</hi> the <hi type="italic">calves of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Hos. xiv. 2</reference>), the <hi type="italic">fruit of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), speaking forth, singing forth, the high praises of our God. This Jonah here promises, that with the sacrifice of thanksgiving he will <hi type="italic">mention the lovingkindness of the Lord,</hi> to his glory, and the encouragement of others. (2.) That he will honour him in his conversation by a punctual performance of his vows, which he made in the fish's belly. Some think it was some work of charity that he vowed, or such a vow as Jacob's was, <hi type="italic">Of all that thou hast given me I will give the tenth unto thee.</hi> More probably his vow was that if God would deliver him he would readily go wherever he should please to send him, though it were to Nineveh. When we smart for deserting our duty it is time to promise that we will adhere to it, and abound in it. Or, perhaps, the sacrifice of thanksgiving is the thing he vowed, and that is it which he will pay, as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17-Ps.116.19">Ps. cxvi. 17-19</reference>. <div eID="gen20334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20335" type="x-p"/> 7. He concludes with an acknowledgment of God as the Saviour of his people: <hi type="italic">Salvation is of the Lord;</hi> it <hi type="italic">belongs to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Ps. iii. 8</reference>. He is the <hi type="italic">God of salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19-Ps.68.20">Ps. lxviii. 19, 20</reference>. He only can work salvation, and he can do it be the danger and distress ever so great; he has promised salvation to his people that trust in him. All the salvations of his church in general, and of particular saints, were wrought by him; he is the <hi type="italic">Saviour of those that believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1 Tim. iv. 10</reference>. Salvation is still of him, as it has always been; from him alone it is to be expected, and on him we are to depend for it. Jonah's experience shall encourage others, in all ages, to trust in God as the God of their salvation; all that read this story shall say with assurance, say with admiration, that <hi type="italic">salvation is of the Lord,</hi> and is sure to all that belongs to him.
entries.9f54e0c546d24f4af5b89926405ee38bd8433478: <div eID="gen20335" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jonah's Deliverance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 840.)</title> <div sID="gen20336" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry <hi type="italic">land.</hi> <div eID="gen20336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20337" type="x-p"/> We have here Jonah's discharge from his imprisonment, and his deliverance from that death which there he was threatened with—his return, though not to life, for he lived in the fish's belly, yet to the <hi type="italic">land of the living,</hi> for from that he seemed to be quite cut off—his resurrection, though not from death, yet from the grave, for surely never man was so buried alive as Jonah was in the fish's belly. His enlargement may be considered, 1. As an instance of God's power over all the creatures. God <hi type="italic">spoke to the fish,</hi> gave him orders to return him, as before he had given him orders to receive him. God speaks to other creatures, and <hi type="italic">it is done;</hi> they are all his ready obedient servants. But to man he <hi type="italic">speaks once, yea, twice, and he perceives it not,</hi> regards it not, but turns a deaf ear to what he says. Note, God has all creatures at his command, makes what use he pleases of them, and serves his own purposes by them. 2. As an instance of God's mercy to a poor penitent, that in his distress prays to him. Jonah had sinned, and had done foolishly, very foolishly; his own backslidings did not correct him, and it appears by his after-conduct that his foolishness was not quite driven from him, no, not by the rod of this correction; and yet, upon his praying, and humbling himself before God, here is a miracle in nature wrought for his deliverance, to intimate what a miracle of grace, free grace, God's reception and entertainment of returning sinners are. When God had him at his mercy he showed him mercy, and did not <hi type="italic">contend for ever.</hi> 3. As a type and figure of Christ's resurrection. He died and was buried, to lay in the grave, as Jonah did, three days and three nights, a prisoner for our debt; but the third day he came forth, as Jonah did, by his messengers to preach repentance, and remission of sins, even to the Gentiles. And thus was another scripture fulfilled, <hi type="italic">After two days he will receive us, and the third day he will raise us up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Hos. vi. 2</reference>. The earth trembled as if full of her burden, as the fish was of Jonah.  <chapter eID="Jonah.2"/> <div eID="gen20337" type="x-p"/>

entries.650a9d843cfedb5188bbaa1732a0ae87db5402b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12686"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1-Jonah.2.10">Jon 2:1-10</reference>. Jonah's Prayer of Faith and Deliverance.</title> <div sID="gen23468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12686"/><hi type="bold">1. his God--</hi>"his" still, though Jonah had fled from Him. Faith enables Jonah now to feel this; just as the returning prodigal says of the Father, from whom he had wandered, "I will arise and go to my Father" (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">Lu 15:18</reference>).<div eID="gen23468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of the fish's belly--</hi>Every place may serve as an oratory. No place is amiss for prayer. Others translate, "when (delivered) out of the fish's belly." English Version is better. <div eID="gen23469" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4511589a838f173dc9f9962dd70543a494f87e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12687"/><div sID="gen23470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12687"/>2. His prayer is partly descriptive and precatory, partly eucharistical. Jonah incorporates with his own language inspired utterances familiar to the Church long before in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.120.1">Psa 120:1</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3">Jon 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.7">Psa 42:7</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">Jon 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1">Psa 69:1</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">Psa 142:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">18:6</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.6">Psa 31:6</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">Psa 116:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.18">18</reference>, and 3:8. Jonah, an inspired man, thus attests both the antiquity and inspiration of the Psalms. It marks the spirit of faith, that Jonah identifies himself with the saints of old, appropriating their experiences as recorded in the Word of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.50">Psa 119:50</reference>). Affliction opens up the mine of Scripture, before seen only on the surface.<div eID="gen23470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of the belly of hell--</hi>Sheol, the unseen world, which the belly of the fish resembled. <div eID="gen23471" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c9c1a8439548eea03804cf0b6ae5ab7b987ced5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12688"/><div sID="gen23472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12688"/><hi type="bold">3. thou hadst cast ... thy billows ... thy waves--</hi>Jonah recognizes the source whence his sufferings came. It was no mere chance, but the hand of God which sent them. Compare Job's similar recognition of God's hand in calamities, <reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>; 2:10; and David's, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.11">2Sa 16:5-11</reference>. <div eID="gen23472" type="x-p"/>
entries.1be60af60b408ae1f0e1a2411571446cdf90b15c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12689"/><div sID="gen23473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12689"/><hi type="bold">4. cast out from thy sight--</hi>that is, from Thy favorable regard. A just retribution on one who had fled "from the presence of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.3">Jon 1:3</reference>). Now that he has got his desire, he feels it to be his bitterest sorrow to be deprived of God's presence, which once he regarded as a burden, and from which he desired to escape. He had turned his back on God; so God turned His back on him, making his sin his punishment.<div eID="gen23473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward thy holy temple--</hi>In the confidence of faith he anticipates yet to see the temple at Jerusalem, the appointed place of worship (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.38">1Ki 8:38</reference>), and there to render thanksgiving [Henderson]. Rather, I think, "Though cast out of Thy sight, I will still with the eye of faith once more look in prayer towards Thy temple at Jerusalem, whither, as Thy earthly throne, Thou hast desired Thy worshippers to direct their prayers." <div eID="gen23474" type="x-p"/>
entries.180e42d8d2e1a3030767f4770d657f3c70a39073: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12690"/><div sID="gen23475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12690"/><hi type="bold">5. even to the soul--</hi>that is, threatening to extinguish the animal life.<div eID="gen23475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weeds--</hi>He felt as if the seaweeds through which he was dragged were wrapped about his head. <div eID="gen23476" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c52775707b1853fc7bebc5101dd2d41dc8f3403: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12691"/><div sID="gen23477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12691"/><hi type="bold">6. bottoms of ... mountains--</hi>their extremities where they terminate in the hidden depths of the sea. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>, "the foundations of the hills" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">Psa 18:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth with her bars was about me--</hi>Earth, the land of the living, is (not "was") shut against me.<div eID="gen23478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>so far as any effort of mine can deliver me.<div eID="gen23479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet hast thou brought up my life from corruption--</hi>rather, "Thou bringest ... from the pit" [Maurer]. As in the previous clauses he expresses the hopelessness of his state, so in this, his sure hope of deliverance through Jehovah's infinite resources. "Against hope he believes in hope," and speaks as if the deliverance were actually being accomplished. Hezekiah seems to have incorporated Jonah's very words in his prayer (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Is 38:17</reference>), just as Jonah appropriated the language of the Psalms. <div eID="gen23480" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f869570f694a76d7ba9b92e629ecf3c35100131: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12692"/><div sID="gen23481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12692"/><hi type="bold">7. soul fainted ... I remembered the Lord--</hi>beautifully exemplifying the triumph of spirit over flesh, of faith over sense (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.26">Psa 73:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">42:6</reference>). For a time troubles shut out hope; but faith revived when Jonah "remembered the Lord," what a gracious God He is, and how now He still preserves his life and consciousness in his dark prison-house.<div eID="gen23481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into thine holy temple--</hi>the temple at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference>). As there he looks in believing prayer towards it, so here he regards his prayer as already heard. <div eID="gen23482" type="x-p"/>
entries.53f26d7fe7f24be5ad95d1def154d70427654f71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12693"/><div sID="gen23483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12693"/><hi type="bold">8. observe lying vanities--</hi>regard or reverence idols, powerless to save (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.6">Psa 31:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy--</hi>Jehovah, the very idea of whom is identified now in Jonah's mind with mercy and loving-kindness. As the Psalmist (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>) styles Him, "my goodness"; God who is to me all beneficence. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.59.17">Psa 59:17</reference>, "the God of my mercy," literally, "my kindness-God." Jonah had "forsaken His own mercy," God, to flee to heathen lands where "lying vanities" (idols) were worshipped. But now, taught by his own preservation in conscious life in the fish's belly, and by the inability of the mariners' idols to lull the storm (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5">Jon 1:5</reference>), estrangement from God seems estrangement from his own happiness (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>; 17:13). Prayer has been restrained in Jonah's case, so that he was "fast asleep" in the midst of danger, heretofore; but now prayer is the sure sign of his return to God. <div eID="gen23484" type="x-p"/>
entries.788345a55846028990425c902a1b6b701212dde8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12694"/><div sID="gen23485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12694"/><hi type="bold">9. I will sacrifice ... thanksgiving--</hi>In the believing anticipation of sure deliverance, he offers thanksgivings already. So Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>) appointed singers to praise the Lord in front of the army before the battle with Moab and Ammon, as if the victory was already gained. God honors such confidence in Him. There is also herein a mark of sanctified affliction, that he vows amendment and thankful obedience (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.67">Psa 119:67</reference>). <div eID="gen23485" type="x-p"/>
entries.71c6f0cd41e8ecaf54e206643fba670d92a6dc23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12695"/><div sID="gen23486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12695"/><hi type="bold">10. upon the dry land--</hi>probably on the coast of Palestine. <chapter eID="Jonah.2"/>

entries.f638e3b5bd9fa26b28e01a8a32ee73ba79455990: <div eID="gen34607" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34608" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34609" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34609" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34608" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34610" type="x-p"/> This chapter (except the first verse and the last, which make a part of the narrative) contains a beautiful prayer or hymn, formed of those devout thoughts which Jonah had in the belly of the great fish, with a thanksgiving for his miraculous deliverance. <div eID="gen34610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34612" type="x-p"/> Then Jonah prayed - out of the fish's belly - This verse makes the first of the second chapter in the Hebrew text. <div eID="gen34612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34613" type="x-p"/> It may be asked, "How could Jonah either pray or breathe in the stomach of the fish?" Very easily, if God so willed it. And let the reader keep this constantly in view; the whole is a miracle, from Jonah's being swallowed by the fish till he was cast ashore by the same animal. It was God that had prepared the great fish. It was the Lord that spake to the fish, and caused it to vomit Jonah upon the dry land. All is miracle.
entries.e00c66de889ef59ba60d680416f757b4f3df2715: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34614" type="x-p"/> Out of the belly of hell - Among the Hebrews שאול sheol means the grave, any deep pit, the place of separate spirits, etc. Here the prophet represents himself as in the bottom of the sea; for so sheol must be understood in this place.
entries.0ae631f3623f74983e558927aaac839222c960e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34615" type="x-p"/> All thy billows and thy waves passed over me - This may be understood literally; while the fish, in whose belly he was, sought its pleasure or sustenance in the paths of the deep, the waves and billows of the sea were rolling above. This line seems borrowed from <reference osisRef="Psa.42.7">Psa 42:7</reference>.
entries.de3d0987326d8d809fd7ea96683ffa664903af4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34616" type="x-p"/> I am cast out of thy sight - See <reference osisRef="Psa.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>. <div eID="gen34616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34617" type="x-p"/> Thy holy temple - Then Jerusalem was not yet destroyed, for the temple was standing.
entries.e65b323a845b707ffbf907e0955932babc89c642: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34618" type="x-p"/> The waters compassed me about even to the soul - So as to seem to deprive me of life. I had no hope left. <div eID="gen34618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34619" type="x-p"/> The weeds were wrapped about my head - This may be understood literally also. He found himself in the fish's stomach, together with sea weeds, and such like marine substances, which the fish had taken for its aliment.
entries.f7a5b4670547d6f354afd4dce318e35acee7ae0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34620" type="x-p"/> I went down to the bottoms of the mountains - This also may be literally understood. The fish followed the slanting base of the mountains, till they terminated in a plain at the bottom of the great deep. <div eID="gen34620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34621" type="x-p"/> The earth with her bars - He represents himself as a prisoner in a dungeon, closed in with bars which he could not remove, and which at first appeared to be for ever, i.e., the place where his life must terminate. <div eID="gen34621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34622" type="x-p"/> Yet hast thou brought up my life - The substance of this poetic prayer was composed while in the fish's belly; but afterwards the prophet appears to have thrown it into its present poetic form, and to have added some circumstances, such as that before us; for he now speaks of his deliverance from this imminent danger of death. "Thou hast brought up my life from corruption."
entries.cc425130abb9d46cc019d7a405ba6a6503f3e829: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34623" type="x-p"/> When my soul fainted - When I had given up all hope of life. <div eID="gen34623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34624" type="x-p"/> My prayer came in unto thee - Here prayer is personified, and is represented as a messenger going from the distressed, and entering into the temple of God, and standing before him. This is a very fine and delicate image. This clause is one of those which I suppose the prophet to have added when he penned this prayer.
entries.98b17451806c5a19b170a22eaab6d2a0808e3349: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34625" type="x-p"/> They that observe lying vanities - They that trust in idols, follow vain predictions, permit themselves to be influenced with foolish fears, so as to induce them to leave the path of obvious duty, forsake their own mercy. In leaving that God who is the Fountain of mercy, they abandon that measure of mercy which he had treasured up for them.
entries.4df155232456798aaef223adc8f5c4198e9b8dcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34626" type="x-p"/> But I will sacrifice unto thee - I will make a sincere vow, which, as soon as my circumstances will permit, I will faithfully execute; and therefore he adds, "I will pay that which I have vowed." <div eID="gen34626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34627" type="x-p"/> Salvation is of the Lord - All deliverance from danger, preservation of life, recovery from sickness, and redemption of the soul from the power, guilt, and pollution of sin, is from Jehovah. He alone is the Savior, he alone is the Deliverer; for all salvation is from the Lord.
entries.d6ec5e1f06b5be85f60ec35582abcf16a47aa4af: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34628" type="x-p"/> And the Lord spake unto the fish - That is, by his influence the fish swam to shore, and cast Jonah on the dry land. So the whole was a miracle from the beginning to the end; and we need not perplex ourselves to find out literal interpretations; such as, "When Jonah was thrown overboard he swam for his life, earnestly praying God to preserve him from drowning; and by his providence he was thrown into a place of fish - a fishing cove, where he was for a time entangled among the weeds, and hardly escaped with his life; and when safe, he composed this poetic prayer, in metaphorical language, which some have wrongly interpreted, by supposing that he was swallowed by a fish; when דג dag should have been understood, as a place of fish, or fishing creek," etc. Now I say the original has no such meaning in the Bible: and this gloss is plainly contrary to the letter of the text; to all sober and rational modes of interpretation; and to the express purpose for which God appears to have wrought this miracle, and to which Jesus Christ himself applies it. For as Jonah was intended for a sign to the Jews of the resurrection of Christ, they were to have the proof of this semiosis, in his lying as long in the heart of the earth as the prophet was in the belly of the fish, and all interpretations of this kind go to deny both the sign and the thing signified. Some men, because they cannot work a miracle themselves, can hardly be persuaded that God can do it. <div eID="gen34628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34629" type="x-p"/> The text, and the use made of it by Christ, most plainly teach us that the prophet was literally swallowed by a fish, by the order of God; and that by the Divine power he was preserved alive, for what is called three days and three nights, in the stomach of the fish; and at the conclusion of the above time that same fish was led by the unseen power of God to the shore, and there compelled to eject the prey that he could neither kill nor digest. And how easy is all this to the almighty power of the Author and Sustainer of life, who has a sovereign, omnipresent, and energetic sway in the heavens and in the earth. But foolish man will affect to be wise; though, in such cases, he appears as the recently born, stupid offspring of the wild ass. It is bad to follow fancy, where there is so much at stake. Both ancients and moderns have grievously trifled with this prophet's narrative; merely because they could not rationally account for the thing, and were unwilling (and why?) to allow any miraculous interference.  <chapter eID="Jonah.2"/> <div eID="gen34629" type="x-p"/>

entries.d11e0279a9e6b0b8b9ac16f1df8028d8f822790d: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1">Jon 2:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“Jonah prayed to Jehovah his God out of the fish’s belly.”</hi> <div eID="gen16491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> The prayer which follows (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2-Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:2-9</reference>) is not a petition for deliverance, but thanksgiving and praise for deliverance already received. It by no means follows from this, however, that Jonah did not utter this prayer till after he had been vomited upon the land, and that v. 10 ought to be inserted before v. 2; but, as the earlier commentators have shown, the fact is rather this, that when Jonah had been swallowed by the fish, and found that he was preserved alive in the fish’s belly, he regarded this as a pledge of his deliverance, for which he praised the Lord. Luther also observes, that “he did not actually utter these very words with his mouth, and arrange them in this orderly manner, in the belly of the fish; but that he here shows what the state of his mind was, and what thoughts he had when he was engaged in this conflict with death.” The expression “his God” (אלהיו) must not be overlooked. He prayed not only to Jehovah, as the heathen sailors also did (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.14">Jon 1:14</reference>), but to Jehovah as his God, from whom he had tried to escape, and whom he now addresses again as his God when in peril of death. “He shows his <hi type="italic">faith</hi> by adoring Him as <hi type="italic">his</hi> God” (Burk). The prayer consists for the most part of reminiscences of passages in the Psalms, which were so exactly suited to Jonah’s circumstances, that he could not have expressed his thoughts and feelings any better in words of his own. It is by no means so “atomically compounded from passages in the Psalms” that there is any ground for pronouncing it “a later production which has been attributed to Jonah,” as Knobel and De Wette do; but it is the simple and natural utterance of a man versed in the Holy Scripture and living in the word of God, and is in perfect accordance with the prophet’s circumstances and the state of his mind. Commencing with the confession, that the Lord has heard his crying to Him in distress (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>), Jonah depicts in two strophes (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3">Jon 2:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5-Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:5-7</reference>) the distress into which he had been brought, and the deliverance out of that destruction which appeared inevitable, and closes in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:9</reference> with a vow of thanksgiving for the deliverance which he had received.
entries.5eb6dd8fbfd0f98f6b0cabbff8a5f8bb30fae00a: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference> <div eID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> 2 <hi type="italic">I cried to Jehovah out of my distress, and He heard me; Out of the womb of hell I cried: Thou heardest my voice!</hi> <div eID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> The first clause recals to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.120.1">Psa 120:1</reference>; but it also shows itself to be an original reproduction of the expression מצּרה לי, which expresses the prophet’s situation in a more pointed manner than בּצּר־לי in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15">Psa 17:1-15</reference> and בּצּרתה לּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.120.1">Psa 120:1</reference>-7. The distress is still more minutely defined in the second hemistich by the expression מבּטן שׁאול, “out of the womb of the nether world.” As a throat or swallow is ascribed to <hi type="italic">she'ōl</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>, so here it is spoken of as having a בטן, or belly. This is not to be taken as referring to the belly of the shark, as Jerome supposes. The expression is a poetical figure used to denote the danger of death, from which there is apparently no escape; like the encompassing with snares of death in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference>, and the bringing up of the soul out of sheol in Psa 30:3. In the last clause the words pass over very appropriately into an address to Jehovah, which is brought out into still greater prominence by the omission of the copula <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>.
entries.50d8460dd68e37daebddb4864fc80769538eb40f: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3-Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> 3 <hi type="italic">Thou castedst me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, And the stream surrounded me; All Thy billows and Thy waves went over me.</hi> <div eID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> 4 <hi type="italic">Then I said, I am thrust away from Thine eyes, Yet I will look again to Thy holy temple.</hi> <div eID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> The more minute description of the peril of death is attached by <hi type="italic">Vav consec.</hi>, to express not sequence in time, but sequence of thought. <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> cast him into the depth of the sea, because the seamen were merely the executors of the punishment inflicted upon him by Jehovah. <hi type="italic">Metsūlâh</hi>, the deep, is defined by “the heart of the seas” as the deepest abyss of the ocean. The plural <hi type="italic">yammı̄m</hi> (seas) is used here with distinct significance, instead of the singular, “into the heart of the <hi type="italic">sea</hi>” (<hi type="italic">yâm</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.8">Exo 15:8</reference>, to express the idea of the boundless ocean (see Dietrich, <hi type="italic">Abhandlung zur hebr. Grammatik</hi>, pp. 16, 17). The next clauses are circumstantial clauses, and mean, so that the current of the sea surrounded me, and all the billows and waves of the sea, which Jehovah had raised into a storm, went over me. <hi type="italic">Nâhâr</hi>, a <hi type="italic">river</hi> or <hi type="italic">stream</hi>, is the streaming or current of the sea, as in Psa 24:2. The words of the second hemistich are a reminiscence of Psa 42:8. What the Korahite singer of that psalm had experienced spiritually, viz., that one wave of trouble after another swept over him, that had the prophet literally experienced. Jonah “does not say, The waves and the billows of the sea went over me; but <hi type="italic">Thy</hi> waves and <hi type="italic">Thy</hi> billows, because he felt in his conscience that the sea with its waves and billows was the servant of God and of His wrath, to punish sin” (Luther). <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference> contains the apodosis to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3">Jon 2:3</reference></hi>: “When Thou castedst me into the deep, then I said (sc., in my heart, i.e., then I thought) that I was banished from the sphere of Thine eyes, i.e., of Thy protection and care.” These words are formed from a reminiscence of <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>, נגרשׁתּי being substituted for the נגרזתּי of the psalm. The second hemistich is attached adversatively. אך, which there is no necessity to alter into אך = איך, as Hitzig supposes, introduces the antithesis in an energetic manner, like אכם elsewhere, in the sense of nevertheless, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.15">Isa 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.16">Psa 49:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference> (cf. Ewald, §354, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). The thought that it is all over with him is met by the confidence of faith that he will still look to the holy temple of the Lord, that is to say, will once more approach the presence of the Lord, to worship before Him in His temple, - an assurance which recals Psa 5:8. <div eID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> The thought that by the grace of the Lord he has been once more miraculously delivered out of the gates of death, and brought to the light of the world, is carried out still further in the following strophe, in entirely new turns of thought.
entries.1de0d4145352e9ff1c37d81a47035fd94d658e63: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5-Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16499" type="x-p"/> 5 <hi type="italic">Waters surrounded me even to the soul: the flood encompassed me, Sea-grass was wound round my head.</hi> <div eID="gen16499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16500" type="x-p"/> 6 <hi type="italic">I went down to the foundations of the mountains; The earth, its bolts were behind me for ever: Then raisedst Thou my life out of the pit, O Jehovah my God.</hi> <div eID="gen16500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16501" type="x-p"/> 7 <hi type="italic">When my soul fainted within me, I thought of Jehovah; And my prayer came to Thee into Thy holy temple.</hi> <div eID="gen16501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16502" type="x-p"/> This strophe opens, like the last, with a description of the peril of death, to set forth still more perfectly the thought of miraculous deliverance which filled the prophet’s mind. The first clause of the fifth verse recals to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">Psa 18:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.69.2">Psa 69:2</reference>; the words “the waters pressed (בּאוּ) even to the soul” (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.2">Psa 69:2</reference>) being simply strengthened by אפפוּני after Psa 18:5. The waters of the sea girt him round about, reaching even to the soul, so that it appeared to be all over with his life. <hi type="italic">Tehōm</hi>, the unfathomable flood of the ocean, surrounded him. <hi type="italic">Sūph</hi>, sedge, i.e., sea-grass, which grows at the bottom of the sea, was bound about his head; so that he had sunk to the very bottom. This thought is expressed still more distinctly in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">Psa 18:6</reference></hi>. קצבי הרים, “the ends of the mountains” (from <hi type="italic">qâtsabh</hi>, to cut off, that which is cut off, then the place where anything is cut off), are their foundations and roots, which lie in the depths of the earth, reaching even to the foundation of the sea (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.16">Psa 18:16</reference>). When he sank into the deep, the earth shut its bolts behind him (הארץ is placed at the head absolutely). The figure of bolts of the earth that were shut behind Jonah, which we only meet with here (בּעד from the phrase סגר הדּלת בּעד, to shut the door behind a person: <reference osisRef="Gen.7.16">Gen 7:16</reference>; 2Ki 4:4-5, 2Ki 4:33; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa 26:20</reference>), has an analogy in the idea which occurs in <reference osisRef="Job.38.10">Job 38:10</reference>, of bolts and doors of the ocean. The bolts of the sea are the walls of the sea-basin, which set bounds to the sea, that it cannot pass over. Consequently the bolts of the earth can only be such barriers as restrain the land from spreading over the sea. These barriers are the weight and force of the waves, which prevent the land from encroaching on the sea. This weight of the waves, or of the great masses of water, which pressed upon Jonah when he had sunk to the bottom of the sea, shut or bolted against him the way back to the earth (the land), just as the bolts that are drawn before the door of a house fasten up the entrance into it; so that the reference is neither to “the rocks jutting out above the water, which prevented any one from ascending from the sea to the land,” nor <hi type="italic">“densissima terrae compages, qua abyssus tecta Jonam in hac constitutum occludebat”</hi> (Marck). Out of this grave the Lord “brought up his life.” <hi type="italic">Shachath</hi> is rendered φθορά, <hi type="italic">corruptio</hi>, by the early translators (lxx, Chald., Syr., Vulg.); and this rendering, which many of the more modern translators entirely reject, is unquestionably the correct one in <reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job 17:14</reference>, where the meaning “pit” is quite unsuitable. But it is by no means warranted in the present instance. The similarity of thought to <reference osisRef="Ps.30.4">Psa 30:4</reference> points rather to the meaning pit = cavern or grave, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>, where <hi type="italic">shachath</hi> is used interchangeably with בּור and שׁאול in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon 2:4</reference> as being perfectly synonymous. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference></hi> is formed after <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference> or <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>, except that נפשׁי is used instead of רוּחי, because Jonah is not speaking of the covering of the spirit with faintness, but of the plunging of the life into night and the darkness of death by drowning in the water. התעטּף, lit., to veil or cover one’s self, hence to sink into night and faintness, to pine away. עלי, upon or in me, inasmuch as the I, as a person, embraces the soul or life (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>). When his soul was about to sink into the night of death, he thought of Jehovah in prayer, and his prayer reached to God in His holy temple, where Jehovah is enthroned as God and King of His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.3">Psa 88:3</reference>). <div eID="gen16502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16503" type="x-p"/> But when prayer reaches to God, then He helps and also saves. This awakens confidence in the Lord, and impels to praise and thanksgiving. These thoughts form the last strophe, with which the Psalm of thanksgiving is appropriately closed.
entries.89e58a6011a5be3f563cf33d832412aaacf26989: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8-Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen16503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16504" type="x-p"/> 8 <hi type="italic">They who hold to false vanities Forsake their own mercy.</hi> <div eID="gen16504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16505" type="x-p"/> 9 <hi type="italic">But I will sacrifice to Thee with the call of thanksgiving. I will pay what I have vowed. Salvation is with Jehovah.</hi> <div eID="gen16505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16506" type="x-p"/> In order to express the thought emphatically, that salvation and deliverance are only to be hoped for from Jehovah the living God, Jonah points to the idolaters, who forfeit their mercy. משׁמּרים הבלי־שׁוא is a reminiscence of Psa 31:7. הבלי־שׁוא, worthless vanities, are all things which man makes into idols or objects of trust. הבלים are, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">Deu 32:21</reference>, false gods or idols. <hi type="italic">Shâmar</hi>, to keep, or, when applied to false gods, to keep to them or reverence them; in Hos 4:10 it is also applied to Jehovah. חסדּם signifies neither <hi type="italic">pietatem suam nor gratiam a Deo ipsis exhibitam</hi>, nor “all the grace and love which they might receive” (Hitzig); but refers to God Himself, as He whose government is pure grace (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.24.27">Gen 24:27</reference>), and might become the grace even of the idolatrous. Jonah, on the contrary, like all the righteous, would sacrifice to the Lord <hi type="italic">beqōl tōdâh</hi>, “with the voice or cry, of thanksgiving,” i.e., would offer his sacrifices with a prayer of sincere thanksgiving (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>), and pay the vow which he had made in his distress (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>). These utterances are founded upon the hope that his deliverance will be effected (Hitzig); and this hope is based upon the fact that “salvation is Jehovah's,” i.e., is in His power, so that He only can grant salvation.
entries.a39967b06ce45ed3290706089192fccc9d56e158: <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.10">Jon 2:10</reference> <hi type="italic">“Then Jehovah spake to the fish, and it vomited Jonah upon the dry land.”</hi> <div eID="gen16506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16507" type="x-p"/> The nature of God’s speaking, or commanding, may be inferred from the words ויּקא וגו. Cyril explains the thought correctly thus: The whale is again impelled by a certain divine and secret power of God, being moved to that which seems good to Him.” The land upon which Jonah was vomited was, of course, the coast of Palestine, probably the country near Joppa. According to <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1">Jon 2:1</reference>, this took place on the third day after he had been swallowed by the fish. Jonah’s Preaching in Nineveh - <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.1-Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:1-10</reference> <div eID="gen16507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16508" type="x-p"/> After Jonah had been punished for his disobedience, and miraculously delivered from death by the mercy of God, he obeyed the renewed command of Jehovah, and preached to the city of Nineveh that it would be destroyed within forty days on account of its sins (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.1-Jonah.3.4">Jon 3:1-4</reference>). But the Ninevites believed in God, and repented in sackcloth and ashes, to avert the threatened destruction (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.5-Jonah.3.9">Jon 3:5-9</reference>); and the Lord spared the city (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon 3:10</reference>).  <chapter eID="Jonah.2"/> <div eID="gen16508" type="x-p"/>

entries.73a04dc15e2885420ecce33963c2f279032a0af4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jonah.2.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jonah.2.1" sID="gen86387" type="section"/> <div sID="gen86388" type="x-p"/>When Jonah says that he <hi type="italic">prayed from the bowels of the fish,</hi> he shows first with what courage of mind he was endued. He had then put on a new heart; for when he was at liberty he thought that he could in a manner escape from God, he became a fugitive from the Lord: but now while inclosed within narrow bounds, he begins to pray, and of his own accord sets himself in God’s presence.<div eID="gen86388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen86389" type="x-p"/>This is a change worthy of being noticed: and hence we may learn how much it profits us to be drawn back often as it were by cords, or to be held tied up with fetters because when we are free we go astray here and there beyond all limits. Jonah, when he was at liberty, became, as we have seen, wanton; but now finding himself restrained by the mighty hand of God, he receives a new mind, and prays from the bowels of the fish <note n="36"> <div sID="gen86390" type="x-p"/> “No place amiss for prayer, <hi type="italic">I will that men pray everywhere;</hi> where ever God casts us we may find a way open heavenwards, if it be now our own fault. Jonah was now in the bottom of the sea, yet out of the depths he cries to God.” — <hi type="italic">M. Henry.</hi> “It may be asked, How could Jonah either pray or breathe in the stomach of a fish? Very easily, if God so willed it. And let the reader keep this constantly in view: the whole is a <hi type="italic">miracle</hi>, from Jonah’s being swallowed by the fish, till he was cast ashore by the same animal. It was God that had <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> the great fish; it was the Lord that <hi type="italic">spake</hi> to the fish, and <hi type="italic">caused</hi> it to vomit Jonah on the dry land. All is miracle.” — <hi type="italic">Adam Clarke.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen86390" type="x-p"/> </note> . But how was it that he directed his petitions then to God, by whose hand he saw that he was so heavily pressed? For God most rigidly handled him; Jonah was in a manner doomed to eternal ruin; the bowels of the fish, as we shall hereafter see, were indeed to him as it were hell or the grave. But in this state of despair Jonah even gathered courage, and was able to retake himself directly to God. It was a wonderful and almost incredible example of faith. Let us then learn to weigh well what is here said; for when the Lord heavily afflicts us, it is then a legitimate and seasonable time for prayer. But we know that the greater part despond, and do not usually offer their prayers freely to God, except their minds be in a calm state; and yet God then especially invites us to himself when we are reduced to extremities. Let this, then, which Jonah declares of himself, come to our minds, — that he cried to God from hell itself: and, at the same time, he assures us that his prayer proceeded from true faith; for he does not simply say that he prayed to <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> but he adds that he was <hi type="italic">his God</hi>; and he speaks with a serious and deeply-reflective mind. Though Jonah then was not only like one dead, but also on the confines of perdition, he yet believed that God would be merciful if he fled to him. We hence see that Jonah prayed not at random, as hypocrites are wont to take God’s name in their mouths when they are in distress, but he prayed in earnest; for he was persuaded that God would be propitious to him.<div eID="gen86389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen86391" type="x-p"/>But we must remember that his prayer was not composed in the words which are here related; but Jonah, while in the bowels of the fish, dwelt on these thoughts in his mind. Hence he relates in this song how he thought and felt; and we shall see that he was then in a state of distraction, as our minds must necessarily be tossed here and there by temptations. For the servants of God do not gain the victory without great struggle. We must fight, and indeed strenuously, that we may conquer. Jonah then in this song shows that he was agitated with great trouble and hard contests: yet this conviction was firmly fixed in his heart, — that God was to be sought, and would not be sought in vain, as he is ever ready to bring help to his people whenever they cry to him.<div eID="gen86391" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jonah.2.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen86387" osisID="Jonah.2.1" type="section"/>
entries.a9d8cc95543e4698f82545f89d3aa487d11c886d:
Then he says, I cried, when I had trouble, to Jehovah, and he answered me. Jonah no doubt relates now, after having come forth from the bowels of the fish, what had happened to him, and he gives thanks to the Lord.
He relates here, as it appears from the preceding, “and he said,” the prayer he offered when in the fish’s bowels, and not a prayer offered after his deliverance. Some have entertained the latter opinion, because some of the verbs here are in the past tense: but this circumstance only shows that he continued to pray from the time when he was swallowed by the fish to the time when he was delivered. It was a continued act. It is the same as though he said, “I have called, and do call on Jehovah.” Marckius, and also Dathius, render the verbs in the present tense, “I call,” etc. The following is a translation according to the view of this prayer, —
3. I call in my distress on Jehovah, and he will answer me; From the belly of the grave I cry, — thou hearest my voice.
4. When thou didst send me to the deep, into the midst of the waters, And the flood surrounded me, — Thy billows and waves over me passed;
5. Then I said, I am banished from the sight of thine eyes; — Yet I will again look towards the temple of thy holiness.
6. Encompass me do the waters to the soul, The deep surrounds me, The sedge is wrapped around my head:
7. To the cuttings off of the mountains have I descended; The earth! Its bars are continually around me: But thou wilt bring from destruction my life, O Jehovah, my God.
8. When overwhelmed within me was my soul, Jehovah did I remember; And come to thee shall my prayer — To the temple of thy holiness.
9. They who regard idols of vanity, Their own mercy forsake:
10. But I, with the voice of praise, will sacrifice to thee, What I have vowed will I fulfill: Salvation belongs to Jehovah.
“The cuttings off,” in verse 7, says Parkhurst, were those parts which were cut off from the mountains at the deluge. The Septuagint has σχισμας — rents-clefts. Roots, bottoms, foundations, have been adopted by some, but not consistently with the meaning of the original word, — “The bars or bolts” of the earth convey the idea of impediments in his way to return to the earth. They were “around” him, or literally “upon” him, בעדי, that is, they were, as it were, closed upon him. — Ed.
This verse then contains two parts, — that Jonah in his trouble fled to God, — and the latter part contains thanksgiving for having been miraculously delivered beyond what flesh could have thought. I cried, he says, in my distress, to Jehovah; I cried out from the bowels of hell, thou hast heard my voice. Jonah, as we shall hereafter see, directed his prayers to God not without great struggle; he contended with many difficulties; but however great the impediments in his way, he still persevered and ceased not from praying. He now tells us that he had not prayed in vain; and, that he might amplify the grace of God, he says, from the bowels of the grave He mentioned distress (angustiam — straitness) in the first clause; but here he more clearly expresses how remarkable and extraordinary had been the kindness of God, that he came forth safe from the bowels of the fish, which were like the bowels of the grave. שאול, shaul, derived from corruption, is called the grave by the Hebrews, and the Latin translator has almost everywhere rendered it hell, (infernum;) and שאול, shaul, is also sometimes taken for hell, that is, the state of the reprobate, because they know that they are condemned by God: it is, however, taken more frequently for the grave; and I am disposed to retain this sense, — that the fish was like the grave. But he means that he was so shut up in the grave, that there was no escape open to him.
What are the bowels of the grave? Even the inside or the recess of the grave itself. When Jonah was in this state, he says, that he was heard by the Lord. It may be proper to repeat again what I have already slightly touched, — that Jonah was not so oppressed, though under the heaviest trial, but that his petitions came forth to God. He prayed as it were from hell, and not simply prayed, for he, at the same time, sets forth his vehemence and ardor by saying, that he cried and cried aloud. Distress, no doubt, extorted from Jonah these urgent entreaties. However this might have been, he did not howl, as the unbelieving are wont to do, who feel their own evils and bitterly complain; and yet they pour forth vain howlings. Jonah here shows himself to be different from them by saying, that he cried and cried aloud to God. It now follows —
Jonah 2:3
3. For thou hadst cast me into the deep, in the midst of the seas; and the floods compassed me about: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me.
3.
